newsitem.title: UK: Forex bulls spurn G7 desire for dollar restraint.
newsitem.headline: Forex bulls spurn G7 desire for dollar restraint.

text.p: This week began with a Group of Seven plea for restraint on the dollar, but the U.S. unit's rise of five pfennigs and nearly four yen in just five sessions leaves little doubt over where market sympathies lie.
"The week started with a G7 statement saying 'enough is enough' and the final market verdict is 'no, it's not'," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
After its meeting in Berlin last weekend, the Group of Seven industrialised nations said exchange rate "misalignments" noted in its April 1995 communique had been corrected.
That statement gave the bulls only brief pause for thought, and the dollar had romped up to a new 34-month high of 1.6935 marks by Wednesday.

A volley of Bundesbank verbal intervention -- together with a Japanese Ministry of Finance threat to act against excessive currency moves -- hauled the dollar down from those heady heights, however, as market fears intensified that the central banks would put their money where their mouths were.

"The pace of the dollar's appreciation has slowed a bit during the course of the week...so you could describe the G7 comments and the subsequent comments from the Bundesbank as being a very modest success," said Stephen King, deputy chief economist at HSBC James Capel.
"But I'd stress the words 'very modest' as it's clear the currency markets are still bullish about the dollar," he added.
Indeed, the dollar hit a fresh four-year high of 124.82 yen in Europe on Friday, well up from Monday's low of 121.00 and raising the spectre of a break of the key psychological 125.
The U.S. currency has gained more than 17 percent -- nearly half of that this year alone -- against the yen since the current bull run began last August.
Dollar/mark's value has risen by 10 percent since the beginning of 1997 and 15.7 percent since August.

Despite the Bundesbank's assertion that the dollar had indeed corrected and that it did not favour further gains, the market's general perception is that Japan is the G3 country most concerned by the dollar's relentless rise, making the Bank of Japan the major focus of intervention jitters.

But analysts say intervention will lack lasting impact unless Japan can persuade the U.S. and Germany to join in, and that may be tough. Economic conditions are more important than FX levels, they say, and those conditions vary between nations.
For Japan, the benefits of a softer yen have now run their course and the impact on import prices have started to hamper profitability in other sectors of the economy, analysts say.
It is also concerned about the impact a weak yen has on both the banking sector and stock prices, and does not want to deter overseas investors, who are big players in the stock market.
Germany and the U.S. are more relaxed about a strong dollar, and could even be cheered by its anti-inflationary effect in the U.S. and the help that gives to German exporters.

"It is only a matter of time before the market launches a more serious assault on the intentions of the G7 and their ability to steer exchange rates, against the flow of fundamentals, with only a half-full kit bag of policy measures," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at DMG.
Fundamentals are key. While they continue to argue for a stronger dollar, that is the way the market will push. And intervention without policy back-up is a weak tool.
"The danger with intervention is that it has to be backed up by changes in domestic policies," said Capel's King.
"Unless the Bundesbank or the Bank of Japan were prepared to sanction a rise in interest rates, or the Fed were prepared to sanction a cut, intervention (impact) will probably be short-lived."
